新井忠雄.note: An inspector of the Shinsengumi and one of Itō’s confidants from the Edo days; he left with Itō’s faction.

加納鵰雄.note: A corporal of the Shinsengumi in Itō’s faction; 鵰雄 is a roster variant for the same man written 道之助 elsewhere (see ch27).

中村半次郎.note: Nakamura Hanjirō (1838–1877), later Kirino Toshiaki: a Satsuma swordsman of the Jigen-ryū reckoned one of the ‘four man-cutters’ of the Bakumatsu, close to Saigō Takamori. He rose to general in the imperial army and fell with Saigō at Shiroyama in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.

与兵衛.note: The keeper of the night saké-shop that gives the chapter its name.

泉涌寺.note: An ancient temple in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, mortuary temple of the imperial house.

戒光寺.note: A sub-temple within the grounds of Sennyū-ji, where Itō’s faction met.

高幡不動.note: A temple of Fudō Myō-ō in the Tama country of Bushū, near Hijikata’s home village of Ishida; the family kept ties to it.

ch34.anchor: Sennyū-ji in the eastern hills of Kyoto
ch34.note: Sennyū-ji, in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, had been the mortuary temple of the imperial house since the thirteenth century, the emperors’ graves lying within its grounds; Kaikō-ji is one of its sub-temples. The meeting-place looks ahead: when Itō’s men formally left the Shinsengumi in the spring of 1867 they styled themselves the Goryō-eji, the ‘Guards of the Imperial Tombs,’ nominally charged with tending these very graves (Emperor Kōmei had just been buried here). Historically grounded.

ch34.anchor: but will the wholesaler sell it that cheap?
ch34.note: Shinohara plays on a proverb, sō wa ton’ya ga orosanai — literally ‘the wholesaler won’t let it go at that price,’ meaning ‘it won’t be that easy.’ He then turns the merchant image into the figure that runs through the chapter: Toshizō is the okeya, the cooper, who binds the loose staves of the corps into one tub with hoops no shock can spring. The pun linking the two tradesmen does not survive into English.

ch34.anchor: the man later known as Kirino Toshiaki
ch34.note: Nakamura Hanjirō took the name Kirino Toshiaki after the Restoration. It is a pointed pairing: the Satsuma man-cutter who steers Itō toward the imperial party here would end, like Saigō, in revolt against the very government he helped to make, dying at Shiroyama in 1877.

Hijikata really did keep a book of haiku under the pen-name Hōgyoku; some forty-one verses survive as the Hōgyoku hokku-shū, compiled in the spring of 1863 before he went up to Kyoto and now held at the Hijikata Toshizō Museum in Hino. The preponderance of spring poems, and of plum blossom, is genuine. Corroborated.

Gidayū-bushi, the dramatic sung narration of the puppet theatre and the kabuki stage, named for the chanter Takemoto Gidayū (1651–1714); a taste for it marks Toshizō as a man of the Edo-country townsman’s world, not the schooled samurai’s.

ch34.anchor: that sold saké and sweet saké
ch34.note: The ‘sweet saké’ is amazake, a thick, barely alcoholic drink of fermented rice, served warm and sold at night-stalls; that Toshizō asks for it in place of wine is what draws Shichiri’s sneer, ‘how gentle of you.’

ch34.anchor: he had loosened his blade in its scabbard
ch34.note: To ‘cut the carp’s mouth’ (koiguchi o kiru) is to break the sword free of the tight fit where the guard meets the scabbard mouth — the first motion of a draw. Done idly, with a laugh, it is a silent threat.

A gō-ō pledge-sheet issued by the Kumano shrines, printed over with the crows sacred to their gods; to swear on one and break the oath was held to call down divine punishment. Shichiri’s calling it ‘old-fashioned’ is the joke of a man who no longer quite believes in it.

Yadake, a slender, hard bamboo whose straight canes were cut for arrow-shafts; a warrior household grew a stand of it as both material and emblem. The farm boy’s planting it, in longing to be a samurai, is preserved in the Hijikata family traditions.
